'''Serrano''' (Serrano: {{lang|ser|Maarrênga'twich}}) is a language in the [[Serran languages|Serran]] branch of the [[Uto-Aztecan]] family spoken by the [[Serrano people|Serrano]] people of [[Southern California]]. The language is closely related to [[Tongva language|Tongva]], [[Tataviam language|Tataviam]], [[Kitanemuk language|Kitanemuk]] and [[Vanyume]], which may be a dialect of Serrano. Serrano has free word order with the only rule being that verbs usually come last.<ref>{{Cite book|title=A Native American Encyclopedia: History, Culture, and Peoples|last=Pritzker|first=Barry|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2000}}</ref>

== Speakers ==
According to [[Ethnologue]], there was 1 speaker in 1994.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ethnologue.com/show_language.asp?code=ser|title=Serrano}}</ref> The last fully fluent speaker was Dorothy Ramon, who died in 2002.<ref name="sbsun">{{Cite news
 |last        = Edwards
 |first       = Andrew
 |title       = Saving the Serrano tongue
 |work        = San Bernardino County Sun
 |access-date  = 2013-05-08
 |date        = 2006-12-05
 |url         = http://www.sbsun.com/ci_4780412
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20130130004041/http://www.sbsun.com/ci_4780412
 |archive-date = 2013-01-30
}}</ref> During the last years of Ramon's life, she worked with linguist Eric Elliot. Together they wrote a book named {{lang|ser|Wayta' Yawa'}} (Always Believe). This book was written in Serrano and English, and talks about the Serrano culture and the life of Ramon, which in turn saved the Serrano language from complete extinction. After Ramon's death, the language is now considered dormant, as revitalization efforts have allowed the language to survive in some form.<ref name=":0" />

Traditionally referring to themselves as Maarrênga'yam meaning "people of Maarra" (Maarra' is considered to be modern day [[Twentynine Palms, California|Twentynine Palms]]) or Yuhaviatam meaning "people of the pines", the Serrano people originally occupied the area near the [[Mojave River]] and [[San Bernardino, California|San Bernardino]] Mountains of Southern California. In 1891 the United States established the [[San Manuel Reservation]] for the Serrano people where many of its last speakers lived. In 1967, Researcher Kenneth Cushman Hill noted that about 6 people still spoke the now dormant language.<ref name=":1">Hill, Kenneth Cushman. "A Grammar of the Serrano Language". ''University of California''. 1967.</ref> As of today,{{when?|date=June 2025}} the nephew of Dorothy Ramon is seen as the last person who is able to speak the language at a fluent level.<ref>{{cite web|title=About – Dorothy Ramon Learning Center |url=https://dorothyramon.org/about/}}</ref>

== Language revitalization ==
The language was at a time considered to be extinct, but there are attempts at reviving it.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ilearn.limuproject.org/iLearn-Course-Portal|title=iLearn Course Portal - iLearn|website=ilearn.limuproject.org|access-date=2012-08-10|archive-date=2018-04-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406230403/http://ilearn.limuproject.org/iLearn-Course-Portal|url-status=dead}}</ref> Both at the [[San Manuel Band of Mission Indians]], and [[Morongo Band of Mission Indians]] [[Indian reservation|reservations]]<ref name = "olson"/> there are efforts now underway to teach the language and the history and culture of the Serrano people. Language teacher Pauline Murillo helped develop an interactive CD ROM for learning Serrano.<ref name = "olson">{{Cite news
| last = David Olson
| title = Pauline Murillo, 76, San Manuel tribal elder
| work = PE.com - Press-Enterprise
| access-date = 2012-08-10
| date = 2011-01-26
| url = http://www.pe.com/local-news/topics/topics-tribes-headlines/20110126-pauline-murillo-76-san-manuel-tribal-elder.ece
| archive-date = 2013-11-02
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131102173215/http://www.pe.com/local-news/topics/topics-tribes-headlines/20110126-pauline-murillo-76-san-manuel-tribal-elder.ece
| url-status = dead
}}</ref> As of 2013, apps and games have been developed, and the San Manuel Band's Serrano Language Revitalization Project (SLRP) seeks to develop further multimedia resources for language learners.<ref>{{cite web
 |title       = San Manuel Band of Serrano Mission Indians: Education
 |access-date  = 2013-05-08
 |url         = http://www.sanmanuel-nsn.gov/education.php.html
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20130415001630/http://www.sanmanuel-nsn.gov/education.php.html
 |archive-date = 2013-04-15
}}</ref> In May 2013, [[Cal State San Bernardino]] announced it would offer Serrano language classes to its students.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news
| last = David Olson
| title = CAL STATE: University offers Serrano language class
| work = Press-Enterprise
| access-date = 2013-06-05
| date = 2013-05-31
| url = http://www.pe.com/local-news/local-news-headlines/20130531-cal-state-university-offers-serrano-language-class.ece
| archive-date = 2013-11-02
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131102173209/http://www.pe.com/local-news/local-news-headlines/20130531-cal-state-university-offers-serrano-language-class.ece
| url-status = dead
}}</ref>

The Limu project offers online courses in Maarrênga' (Morongo Band "Serrano" dialect) and Yuhaviat (San Manuel Band "Serrano" dialect).<ref>{{cite web
| title = iLearn Course Portal - iLearn. Serrano Dialects Maarrenga' (Morongo Band "Serrano" dialect); Yuhaviat (Santos Manuel Band "Serrano" dialect)
| work = The Limu Project
| access-date = 2013-05-08
| url = http://ilearn.limuproject.org/iLearn-Course-Portal
| archive-date = 2018-04-06
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180406230403/http://ilearn.limuproject.org/iLearn-Course-Portal
| url-status = dead
}}</ref>

The Serrano language was traditionally a spoken language; an alphabet was not used until the 1990s. A new alphabet, with 47 letters, including the [[glottal stops|glottal stop]], was developed starting in 2005.<ref name = "sbsun"/>

The Endangered Languages Project lists Serrano as in the "awakening" stage, meaning that the language has lost its native and fluent speakers and can be considered "extinct" but has revitalization projects underway to preserve knowledge of the language and the Serrano people.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Serrano {{!}} Endangered Languages Project |url=https://www.endangeredlanguages.com/elp-language/1518 |access-date=2025-12-07 |website=www.endangeredlanguages.com}}</ref>

The [[University of California, Los Angeles]] provides a recording of a Serrano speaker reading a word list.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.endangeredlanguages.com/lang/1518/samples/5531|title=Endangered Languages Project - Serrano - ser_word-list_1980_01|website=www.endangeredlanguages.com}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==Morphology==
Serrano is an [[agglutinative]] language, where words use suffix complexes for a variety of purposes with several [[morpheme]]s strung together.
